title: How I Built an AI-Powered Document Intelligence Platform Using Next.js, FastAPI, RAG and MCP
summary:
Introduction

In today's rapidly evolving world of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond experimenting with Large Language Models (LLMs) and explore how AI can be integrated into real-world business workflows. My goal was to understand how AI systems can process unstructured data, extract meaningful information, validate results, and support decision-making while maintaining reliability and human oversight.

As organizations continue to handle growing volumes of invoices, reports, contracts, and other business documents, manual processing can become time-consuming and difficult to manage efficiently. I wanted to explore how modern AI technologies could help simplify these processes by combining intelligent document processing, automated workflows, and context-aware information retrieval into a single application.

That motivation led me to build the AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform.

The idea was to create more than a traditional document management system. I wanted to explore how Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and agentic workflows could work together to classify documents, extract structured information, apply validation rules, and make document content accessible through an AI-powered assistant. At the same time, I wanted to ensure that important business decisions remained under human control through a human-in-the-loop approval workflow.

To bring these ideas together, I worked with technologies including Next.js, TypeScript, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, LangChain, LangGraph, ChromaDB, OpenAI, Model Context Protocol (MCP), AWS S3, and Docker. Each technology helped me explore a different aspect of building a complete AI-powered application, from frontend development and backend API design to document retrieval, workflow orchestration, persistent storage, and external tool integration.

Throughout the development process, I explored how to connect AI capabilities with conventional software engineering practices such as authentication, role-based access control, document lifecycle management, and audit logging. This helped me better understand that building a useful AI application involves more than integrating an LLM; it requires designing a complete system around data quality, security, workflow reliability, and accountability.

In this article, I'll walk through the motivation behind the project, its architecture, the document processing pipeline, the RAG-powered assistant, the human approval workflow, the technologies I used, and the key lessons I learned while building the platform.

Project Repositories

  • Frontend: https://github.com/Madesh-cse/AI-Document-Approval-system-frontend
  • Backend: https://github.com/Madesh-cse/AI-Document-Approval-system-backend

From Documents to Decisions: Building an AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform

Turning unstructured documents into actionable insights with LLMs, agentic workflows, RAG, and human-in-the-loop approval.

Every organization works with documents— invoices, contracts, reports, and business records. But behind every document lies a time-consuming process: extracting information, validating it, routing it to the right person, and tracking decisions.

Traditional document management systems help store and organize files, but they don't always understand their contents or automate the decisions that follow.

I wanted to explore how AI could bridge this gap, so I built an AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform that combines document processing, intelligent retrieval, workflow automation, and human oversight in one system.

In this article, I'll walk through the architecture, key technologies, workflow design, and engineering decisions behind the project.

What Does the Platform Do?

The platform transforms uploaded documents into structured, searchable, and reviewable information.

Instead of manually reading every document and transferring its details into a system, users can upload a document and let the application handle the initial processing.

The platform supports:

  • Intelligent document processing: Classifies documents and extracts relevant information.
  • Validation guardrails: Checks extracted data before it proceeds through the workflow.
  • Human-in-the-loop approval: Allows managers to review, approve, or reject documents.
  • Document-specific AI assistant: Answers questions using the contents of a selected document.
  • Role-based access control: Separates permissions for administrators, managers, and employees.
  • Workflow automation: Uses MCP-based Google Calendar integration to schedule approval reviews.
  • Auditable document lifecycle: Tracks document status and approval activity.

The objective isn't to replace human decision-makers. It's to reduce repetitive work while keeping important decisions accountable.

Technology Stack

I selected the following technologies to build the application across the frontend, backend, AI, storage, and deployment layers.

Technology Purpose
Next.js, TypeScript Frontend and application interface
Tailwind CSS Responsive UI styling
Python, FastAPI Backend APIs and application logic
PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy Relational data persistence and ORM
LangChain LLM integration and retrieval components
LangGraph Stateful, multi-step AI workflows
OpenAI Language understanding, extraction, and question answering
ChromaDB Vector storage for document retrieval
AWS S3 Persistent document storage
MCP Integration with external tools, including Google Calendar
Docker Containerized application setup

Each component has a specific responsibility, helping keep the system modular and easier to maintain.

1. Designing the Document Processing Pipeline

A document upload is only the beginning. The system needs to turn that file into information that can be validated, searched, and reviewed.

I designed the processing workflow around the following stages:

Upload → Classification → Information Extraction → Validation → Indexing → Human Review → Approval or Rejection

Step 1: Document upload

Users upload supported PDF, JPG, or PNG documents. The backend validates the file type and size before processing it.

The original document is stored in AWS S3, while the application's database maintains the associated metadata and workflow state.

Step 2: Classification and extraction

The AI processing layer identifies the document category and extracts relevant fields into a structured representation.

For example, an invoice may contain:

  • Invoice number
  • Vendor name
  • Invoice date
  • Total amount
  • Payment-related details

Structured output makes it easier for downstream application logic to validate and use the information.

Step 3: Validation guardrails

LLM output should not automatically be treated as correct.

The validation layer checks whether the extracted information satisfies the application's requirements. Invalid or incomplete data can be flagged for additional review rather than silently passing through the workflow.

This distinction is important: an AI model can interpret information, but application rules must determine whether that information is acceptable.

Step 4: Human review

After processing, the document can enter a pending-review state.

Managers can inspect the extracted information and supporting document before approving or rejecting it. This creates a clear boundary between AI-assisted preparation and human authorization.

2. Why I Used LangGraph for Agentic Workflows

A document workflow is not always a simple sequence of LLM calls. Different outcomes may require different actions.

For example, a document with missing information should not follow exactly the same path as a document that has passed every validation check.

LangGraph helps represent this kind of process as a stateful graph, where nodes perform operations and edges determine what happens next.

In this project, the workflow separates responsibilities such as:

  • Document processing
  • Validation
  • Content indexing
  • Review scheduling
  • Human approval

This makes the workflow easier to understand and extend than placing every operation inside one large function.

It also provides a foundation for conditional routing, error handling, and human-in-the-loop interruptions.

One important design principle guided this implementation: agentic workflows should have clearly defined responsibilities and controlled transitions, not unrestricted autonomy.

3. Building a Document-Specific RAG Assistant

One of the most useful features is the AI assistant that answers questions about an uploaded document.

A general-purpose language model may generate a plausible answer without knowing the contents of a particular invoice or contract. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by retrieving relevant document content before generating an answer.

Here's how the retrieval pipeline works:

  1. Extract text from the uploaded document.
  2. Split the text into manageable chunks.
  3. Generate embeddings for those chunks.
  4. Store the vectors and associated metadata in ChromaDB.
  5. Convert a user's question into a retrieval query.
  6. Retrieve relevant document chunks.
  7. Provide the retrieved context to the language model to generate an answer.

For example, a user might ask:

“What is the total amount on this invoice, and which vendor issued it?”

Rather than relying only on the model's general knowledge, the assistant retrieves relevant information from the selected document and uses it to formulate the response.

Why document-specific retrieval matters

The assistant is designed to answer questions within the context of the selected document. This helps reduce irrelevant retrieval and makes responses more useful for document analysis.

It is also important to recognize that RAG does not eliminate hallucinations. Retrieval quality, source relevance, prompt design, and output validation all influence answer reliability.

For a production-ready implementation, I would further strengthen the assistant with explicit source citations, retrieval confidence checks, and tests for unsupported answers.

4. Keeping Humans in the Loop

Automation is valuable, but business workflows often require accountability.

Consider an invoice with an unexpected total or incomplete vendor information. Automatically approving it because an AI model returned a confident answer would introduce unnecessary risk.

The platform therefore separates the processing result from the approval decision.

  • The AI prepares and validates information.
  • The application maintains the document's workflow status.
  • The manager reviews the document.
  • The manager makes the approval or rejection decision.
  • The system records relevant lifecycle and audit information.

This design supports transparency and makes it easier to understand what happened to a document throughout its lifecycle.

Human review is not merely an additional screen in the application. It is an architectural control over how AI-generated information becomes an operational decision.

🔗 5. Connecting AI Workflows to External Tools with MCP

AI applications become more useful when they can interact with tools beyond the language model itself.

I integrated the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with Google Calendar to support scheduling approval reviews.

The workflow connects document processing with a real-world follow-up action: when a review needs to be scheduled, the application can use the calendar integration to create an event.

This demonstrates how an AI-enabled workflow can go beyond generating text and coordinate with an external service.

However, tool integration also introduces responsibilities around authorization, input validation, failure handling, and duplicate actions. These need to be handled carefully when expanding the integration.

6. Security, Storage, and Application Architecture

AI capabilities are only one part of a reliable document platform. The surrounding application needs to manage access, data, and workflow state correctly.

Authentication and role-based access control

I implemented secure authentication and role-based access control for administrators, managers, and employees.

Permissions determine which document operations are available to different roles. This is particularly important when documents contain business or financial information.

Database and file storage

PostgreSQL stores structured application data, with SQLAlchemy providing the ORM layer. AWS S3 handles persistent document storage.

Separating file storage from relational metadata makes the responsibilities of each component clearer.

Docker

Docker provides a consistent containerized setup, helping reduce differences between development and deployment environments.

These infrastructure decisions complement the AI workflow by giving the application a foundation for data persistence, access management, and maintainability.

7. Engineering Lessons and Trade-Offs

Building this project reinforced several important lessons about AI application development.

1. Structured output is not the same as validated output.

A model can return correctly formatted JSON while still producing incorrect values. Schema validation and business rules remain essential.

2. Retrieval quality matters as much as generation quality.

A strong language model cannot reliably answer a document-specific question if the relevant content was not retrieved. Chunking, embeddings, metadata, and retrieval strategy all influence the result.

3. Workflow state deserves explicit design.

Document statuses and approval transitions should be managed consistently. AI processing, database updates, and external tool calls should not be treated as one indivisible operation.

4. Automation should be proportional to risk.

Classification and information extraction are good candidates for automation. High-impact business approvals often benefit from human authorization.

5. Integrations create failure scenarios.

Storage operations, database transactions, model calls, and calendar events can fail independently. Retry policies, clear error states, and idempotent operations are important considerations as a system grows.

These lessons apply far beyond document processing. They are relevant to AI-powered support systems, compliance workflows, enterprise search, and other applications that combine probabilistic models with deterministic business logic.

What's Next?

There are several directions in which I would like to evolve the platform:

  • Improve extraction evaluation with representative test documents and field-level accuracy metrics.
  • Add stronger source citations and confidence-aware handling to document question answering.
  • Expand workflow observability with structured logs, execution traces, and failure metrics.
  • Introduce more comprehensive automated tests for permissions, approval transitions, and AI outputs.
  • Add asynchronous processing for larger document workloads.
  • Strengthen security with more granular authorization, retention policies, and audit controls.

The next stage is not simply adding more AI features. It is measuring reliability and making the existing workflow more robust.



Final Thoughts

Building this platform helped me explore how modern AI components can work together inside a practical software application.

LangChain and LangGraph provide building blocks for AI integration and stateful workflows. RAG connects language-model responses to document content. MCP enables interaction with external tools. Meanwhile, authentication, authorization, validation, storage, and audit logging provide the application-level controls needed around those capabilities.

The most important takeaway is that building a useful AI application requires more than connecting an LLM to an API. It requires designing the complete system around data quality, workflow state, security, and human accountability.

This project represents my continued exploration of AI engineering: moving beyond isolated model experiments and building applications that integrate AI into real software workflows.

I'd love to hear from other developers:

When building AI-powered business applications, where do you draw the line between autonomous processing and mandatory human approval?

title: My 1B model renamed one file to another file's name — the fix was a provenance guard
summary:
My Downloads folder had 599 loose files in it — 101 PDFs, 79 spreadsheets, 129 images, and a folder full of things called img.png, fp.jpeg and 1762857107887_floop-plan-4.png. I had been closing that tab for months.

So for this week's Hacktoberfest challenge ("build something with open-source AI that rewards laziness") I wrote Tidy Sloth: a local file tidier that sorts a mess into folders and gives files names a human can actually read. Python standard library, Ollama, no cloud, no API key.

It works. But the interesting part isn't the sorting. It's that a 1-billion-parameter model confidently renamed one file to a completely different file's name, and the fix was not a better prompt.

The sloth is the architecture, not the mascot

Sloths are slow because speed costs energy. A file tidier has the same economics: most files are obvious, and asking a language model about them is wasted work.

So the pipeline spends tokens like they're calories:

title: I Found Creating README Files Harder Than Expected, So I Built My Own Solution
summary:
As developers, we spend a lot of time building projects. But when it comes to explaining those projects to others, things can get surprisingly difficult.

I'm talking about README files.

A README is often the first thing someone sees when they visit your GitHub repository. It explains what your project does, how to install it, how to use it, and why someone might want to contribute.

But creating a README that is both informative and visually appealing? That's a different story.

The Problem

When I started creating README files for my own projects, I wanted them to look professional and be easy to understand.

I explored different websites and tools to make the process easier. AI tools could help generate content, and Markdown editors made writing and previewing easier.

However, I still felt that the overall workflow could be better.

I wanted a dedicated desktop application where I could work with Markdown more comfortably without constantly switching between different tools.

That made me think:

What if I built a tool to make working with Markdown documentation a better experience?

Turning an Idea Into a Project

Instead of just thinking about it, I started building VisualMark Studio (VMS).

VMS is an open-source desktop application built with Electron, designed to make working with Markdown more convenient.

My goal wasn't simply to create another editor. I wanted to build something useful for developers who regularly write documentation, create GitHub README files, or work with Markdown.

Building it has been a learning experience in itself. Beyond implementing features, I've had to deal with bugs, improve the user experience, test the application, and keep refining the project.

It's a reminder that building software isn't just about making something work. It's also about making it useful and reliable.

What Makes VisualMark Studio Different?

A few things matter to me about this project:

  • Desktop experience: A dedicated Electron application for working with Markdown.
  • Automatic updates: This has been part of VMS since version 1.0.0, allowing the application to update without users having to download it again from the repository for every release.
  • Free and open source: VMS is free, and my commitment is to keep it that way.
  • Community-driven improvement: The source code is publicly available, and developers can explore the project, report issues, and contribute.

I'm continuing to improve the application, and I know there is still room to make it better.

The Journey Doesn't End Here

One thing I've learned from building VMS is that solving a problem you personally experience is a great starting point. But understanding how other developers experience that same problem is equally important.

That's why I'd like to hear from the DEV Community.

I'd love to know:

  1. Do you find creating and maintaining GitHub README files difficult?
  2. Do you prefer online Markdown tools, VS Code, or dedicated desktop applications?
  3. What features would make your Markdown documentation workflow easier?

I'd genuinely appreciate your thoughts, suggestions, and constructive criticism.

Check Out VisualMark Studio

GitHub repository: VisualMark Studio

If you want to use the VisualMark Studio, you can get a pre-built V1.1.4 is available in the repo

And also there is a major update is coming to VisualMark Studio which includes some quality updates, safety & security upgrade and new features in few days. I hope guys like it.

And this my demo website for the VisualMark Studio Web,still work in progress stage.

If you're interested in the project, feel free to explore the source code, try the application, or share your feedback.

Thanks for reading!

title: Three settings that decide whether EmbeddingGemma 2 search works on your GPU
summary:
EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model Google DeepMind released on 6 October under Apache 2.0. An embedding model turns an input into a list of numbers (768 here) so that similar meanings get nearby lists, and search becomes "find the nearest list". This one takes text, images, video and audio into the same space, from a 1.5 GB download of 740M parameters.

We served it on a 16 GB NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada on our own cloud. Loading it was easy. Three settings decided whether the vectors were correct and latency reasonable, so settle them before you write the indexing job.

The number format that fails without an error

GPUs can store numbers in compact 16-bit formats, float16 and bfloat16, to halve memory. Google's model card (the documentation shipped with the weights) allows only bfloat16 or float32. In float16, some values inside the network get too large to represent, and the card says you get NaN or subtly degraded embeddings with no exception. In a search index that means no crash, just worse rankings.

The card's suggested selection fits in one line:

# never float16: NaN or quietly wrong vectors, no exception
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() else torch.float32

On a GPU without native bfloat16, the float32 fallback needs twice the memory. All our runs used a safe format, so the float16 failure is Google's warning, not something we reproduced. That run is our next test. Log which dtype your stack actually loads.

Photos were slow because the container saw 64 cores

Our first backend handled images two to five times slower than it should have. A profiler showed about 72 ms of GPU work per image against 0.33 to 0.44 seconds of CPU preprocessing. The container's CPU quota (the share of the host's processors it may use, set through Linux cgroups) was about 7 cores, but PyTorch counted the host's 64 and started 64 threads to fight over 7.

Limiting threads to the quota took a single image from 531 to 111 ms, eight images from 4,333 to 867 ms, and a 6-second video clip from 754 to 307 ms. Text and audio stayed almost flat, so a text-only benchmark never shows this.

Our example backend derives the thread count from the cgroup quota. Without a quota, you set it by hand. We verified this on one container only, so time CPU preprocessing and GPU encoding separately, per input type, on yours.

Freed GPU memory stays reserved

The complete model occupied 1.4 GB of GPU memory, or 0.5 GB with only the text part loaded. Single-input requests peaked at 2.6 GB. Batching is where it grows: eight documents of roughly 6,000 tokens each (a token is about a word or part of one) in one request peaked near 10 GB.

The surprise came afterwards. PyTorch caches released GPU memory for reuse, so the process held 11.6 GB until a restart. Calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() after very large requests fixed it: the same batch now leaves the process at 1.6 GB. For bulk indexing, size the GPU for your biggest batch.

Shorter vectors: same speed, some quality loss

Google trained the model with Matryoshka Representation Learning, so the first 512, 256 or 128 numbers of each vector work as a smaller embedding. Truncating was not faster for us (34 to 35 ms per query at every size). Only storage and payload shrink.

The quality cost depends on the input type, per the model card:

Benchmark 768 256 128
MTEB multilingual v2 (text) 61.36 60.41 57.89
MMEB v2 (images and video) 59.01 56.24 45.65
MSEB retrieval (speech) 69.54 66.76 56.71

The card calls 256 close to lossless. At 128, text holds, but image and video search drops by almost a quarter, so the card keeps 128 for text. Re-normalize each vector after cutting it (scale it back to length 1), and embed queries and documents at the same size. Our EmbeddingGemma 2 measurements of VRAM and latency per input type show what each option costs on a 16 GB card.

What the search test does and does not show

Our test index had twelve files and zero text: photos, short videos and spoken recordings. Six English queries each ranked the correct file first. "How to knead bread dough" matched a Spanish recording of a bread recipe. We generated all twelve files, so this confirms the cross-modal pipeline runs end to end, not how the model compares with others. The images came from Sperid Labs' Iris-3B, which we ran in an earlier test of the Iris-3B image model, and the voices from Pocket TTS.

On serving: vLLM, the open-source inference server, did not support this model in version 0.31.0 when we checked, not even for text, so we wrote a small Python backend on sentence-transformers. Google's launch post names vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp as supported tooling, so check current versions first. The complete EmbeddingGemma 2 deployment write-up, with latency and VRAM tables for every input type, covers the request format, start-up times and all five problems we ran into.

Credits

Google DeepMind built EmbeddingGemma 2: the model, its image, video and audio components, the benchmark results and the float16 warning. Sahil Dua and Henrique Schechter Vera wrote the launch post. The truncatable vectors rely on Matryoshka Representation Learning by Kusupati and colleagues. Hugging Face transformers supports the model from version 5.19.0, and sentence-transformers runs it. PyAV decoded our audio and video, and ffmpeg cut the clips. We wrote the backend, took the measurements and fixed the thread count and the memory cache.

The backend code, the SDK example and every number above are in the EmbeddingGemma 2 deployment article on inferencekey.com.

title: SlothDesk — Local-First AI Downloads Organizer: Less sorting. More living.
summary:
This is a submission for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

🦥 What I Built

Existing tools typically fall into two extremes:

  1. Dumb regex scripts that break on edge cases and force rigid naming conventions.
  2. Cloud AI utilities that upload your private documents and filenames to third-party APIs, charging recurring subscription fees.

├── Images/
├── Videos/
├── Audio/
├── Archives/
├── Code/
└── Other/

Many AI file organizers give the model direct write tools or shell access (CodeAgent, shutil.rmtree, os.rename). If the model hallucinates or encounters ambiguous context, files can be permanently destroyed.

    • get_allowed_categories()
    • validate_category(category)

title: DeepSeek Just Open-Sourced Its Production Inference Stack — Here's What I'd Steal for My Own Serving Setup
summary:
DeepSeek Just Open-Sourced Its Production Inference Stack — Here's What I'd Steal for My Own Serving Setup

Research note — VisionQuantech, October 22, 2026

On October 20, DeepSeek published DeepInfer on GitHub under Apache 2.0 — the actual inference framework it says powers its large-scale production services, targeting DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Not a paper. The working stack. Here's the builder's read: what it is, what to take from it, and what its limits teach you about serving LLMs at scale.

TL;DR

  • What: production inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Apache 2.0
  • Hardware: NVIDIA SM100 (Blackwell) + Huawei Ascend 950 — first-class support for both in one codebase
  • Mode: offline inference only; no KV-cache system, no prefill/decode disaggregation, no replica load balancing
  • Signature features: DSpark speculative decoding with confidence-scheduled verification, async zero-overhead scheduling, batch-invariant deterministic inference, structured outputs (regex/JSON schema/EBNF)
  • Production numbers (DeepSeek's, unverified): 155 trillion tokens/day per cluster, 96% input cache hit rate, ~400ms TTFT, 230 tok/s output (300 for code), ~$38/GPU-hour revenue at valley pricing

The quick start that matters

Build requirements: Linux, GCC 13+, Python 3.12, CUDA 13 (NVIDIA) or CANN 9.2 (Ascend). Default checkpoint deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 downloads into the Hugging Face cache on first run. The shape of a first run, from the README's documented flow:

git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer.git
cd DeepInfer

# empty Python 3.12 environment first, per the README
export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia   # or: ascend (Huawei Ascend 950)
./build.sh

# runs the default checkpoint, downloaded to the Hugging Face cache on first run
python examples/offline_inference.py

# or point at a local copy of the weights
DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 python examples/offline_inference.py

Two things to notice. First, structured outputs are a first-class citizen — regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar constraints built into the sampler, not bolted on with a wrapper. If your pipeline parses LLM output (and whose doesn't), grammar-constrained generation is the single highest-ROI feature to lift from this release into your own stack.

Second, deterministic sampling + batch-invariant inference: identical inputs produce identical outputs regardless of batch composition. If you've ever debugged a flaky eval that only fails under load, you know why this exists. It's currently NVIDIA-only — porting the batch-invariant path is one of the obvious community contributions this release invites.

For the reference evals, the repo ships an eval folder with driver scripts (bash eval/aime/run.sh); datasets aren't downloaded for you, HLE and GPQA are gated on Hugging Face, and scoring defaults to an LLM judge service (set the EVAL_JUDGE_* variables or use the rule-based judge for AIME/GPQA). Security note before you build: this compiles vendored operators and pulls multi-gigabyte weights — use a disposable machine or container, and read build.sh first.

DSpark: speculative decoding, done the production way

The feature I'd study first. Speculative decoding drafts several tokens ahead and verifies them in one pass. DeepInfer's DSpark adds confidence-scheduled verification: the draft step emits tokens plus confidence estimates, and the verifier uses those estimates to schedule what gets checked. Default maximum draft length is 5.

Why this is the production-correct version of an old trick: naive speculative decoding wastes compute verifying drafts that were obviously going to be rejected. Confidence-scheduled verification skips the doomed checks. This is the kind of optimization that only survives contact with real traffic — and it's exactly the kind of optimization frontier labs never used to share.

The architecture checklist, as a syllabus

The README's component list is worth treating as a checklist for any serious inference setup:

  1. Kernels: FlashMLA (attention), DeepGEMM, DeepEP (MoE communication), TileKernels, DeepSelect, custom TileLang kernels. The MoE kernels are the load-bearing ones — V4.1-Flash is an MoE model, and expert-parallelism efficiency is what separates a cheap serve from an expensive one.
  2. Parallelism: attention data-parallel with balanced context parallelism, MoE expert-parallel with EPLB (expert load balancing). If you're serving any MoE model, EPLB is the mechanism to study.
  3. SWA bounded replay for long-context efficiency.
  4. Batch-invariant + deterministic modes for reproducible evals.

And the lineage credit: "originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM." Reading between the lines, this is a map of which open-source serving ideas survived production hardening. vLLM won the architecture lottery here.

What the release deliberately excludes — and why that's a lesson

DeepInfer ships without a KV-cache system, without prefill/decode disaggregation, without load balancing across data-parallel replicas. The README says so plainly. That's not an omission — it's the honest boundary between "inference engine" (what you got) and "serving stack" (what DeepSeek runs). Benchmarks were measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode, per MarkTechPost's reading.

The lesson for builders: serving at 155T tokens/day is 20% inference engine, 80% everything around it — caching, disaggregation, scheduling policy, fleet management. Don't mistake the open-sourced 20% for the whole machine. But do treat it as the first time anyone has shown you the 20% in complete working form.

The dual-silicon bet

The headline the press underplayed: one codebase, NVIDIA SM100 and Huawei Ascend 950, same first-class support. DeepSeek said last week it plans to pre-train on Huawei silicon by end of 2026. A unified serving framework is what makes that plan executable — same model, same serving code, whichever chips you can buy. In an export-control world, hardware-agnostic serving is infrastructure strategy, not generosity.

The repo reportedly crossed 8,000 GitHub stars within hours — a day after the US DHS banned DeepSeek from federal agencies. Code doesn't clear customs.

What to actually do with this

  1. Clone it and read the scheduler. The async batch scheduler and DSpark verification logic are the highest-value code in the repo.
  2. Port batch-invariant inference to your stack if you run evals under load.
  3. Adopt grammar-constrained generation (regex/JSON schema/EBNF) as a default pattern in your pipelines.
  4. Don't try to rebuild DeepSeek's economics from this repo alone — the 96% cache hit rate comes from their traffic, not their code.

The gap between a systems paper and a production stack is where ML infra teams spend their years. DeepSeek just handed you a worked example of how to cross it. Read it like a syllabus.

DeepInfer ships without a KV-cache system, without prefill/decode disaggregation, without load balancing across data-parallel replicas. The README says so plainly. That's not an omission — it's the honest boundary between "inference engine" (what you got) and "serving stack" (what DeepSeek runs). Benchmarks were measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode, per MarkTechPost's reading.

The lesson for builders: serving at 155T tokens/day is 20% inference engine, 80% everything around it — caching, disaggregation, scheduling policy, fleet management. Don't mistake the open-sourced 20% for the whole machine. But do treat it as the first time anyone has shown you the 20% in complete working form.

The dual-silicon bet

The headline the press underplayed: one codebase, NVIDIA SM100 and Huawei Ascend 950, same first-class support. DeepSeek said last week it plans to pre-train on Huawei silicon by end of 2026. A unified serving framework is what makes that plan executable — same model, same serving code, whichever chips you can buy. In an export-control world, hardware-agnostic serving is infrastructure strategy, not generosity.

The repo reportedly crossed 8,000 GitHub stars within hours — a day after the US DHS banned DeepSeek from federal agencies. Code doesn't clear customs.

What to actually do with this

  1. Clone it and read the scheduler. The async batch scheduler and DSpark verification logic are the highest-value code in the repo.
  2. Port batch-invariant inference to your stack if you run evals under load.
  3. Adopt grammar-constrained generation (regex/JSON schema/EBNF) as a default pattern in your pipelines.
  4. Don't try to rebuild DeepSeek's economics from this repo alone — the 96% cache hit rate comes from their traffic, not their code.

The gap between a systems paper and a production stack is where ML infra teams spend their years. DeepSeek just handed you a worked example of how to cross it. Read it like a syllabus.

title: I built an on-device overlay to debug Firebase Analytics events (no cable, no logcat)
summary:
The problem

Checking analytics events on Android usually means plugging in a cable, filtering logcat, or setting up Firebase DebugView. Testers can't easily do that on their own phones, so wrong events (bad names, too many params) often get found after release.

What Event Box does

Event Box is a small open-source library. A floating bubble sits on top of your app. Tap it and a panel shows events as they fire: number, time, name and params. Think of it as Firebase DebugView on the device itself.

  • ⚠ Firebase limit warnings: any event that breaks a rule (event name length, param count, value length, user property limits) gets a warning icon, and tapping it shows the exact reason.
  • Resizable, pinnable panel: draggable, snaps to the screen edge, shows an unread badge.
  • Background overlay mode (opt-in): stays visible in recents (needs SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW in your debug manifest).
  • Safe by design: a kill switch, timed sessions that end by themselves, and logging that never throws into your app.
  • Kotlin and Java, minSdk 21, ships its own R8 rules, and events are exposed as StateFlow.

Setup 

implementation("com.github.JpOriginDev:event-box:1.3.0")  // via JitPack

// Application.onCreate()
OGEventBoxLog.setDebugModeEnabled(BuildConfig.DEBUG)
    .setDebugModeDurationHours(0.5)
    .install(this)

// somewhere in your app (hidden gesture, debug menu)
OGEventBoxLog.setEnabled(context, true)

OGEventBoxLog.log("purchase", bundle)

One-call wrapper (no double logging)

Instead of calling OGEventBoxLog.log() next to every analytics call, wrap your SDK once. It has no analytics dependency of its own, so it works with Firebase, Amplitude, Mixpanel or anything else:

val analytics = OGEventBoxAnalytics.wrap(
    eventSink = { name, params -> firebaseAnalytics.logEvent(name, params) },
    userPropertySink = { name, value -> firebaseAnalytics.setUserProperty(name, value) }
)

analytics.logEvent("purchase", bundle)

The event goes to Event Box first (it never throws), then to your SDK. While the box is off, only your SDK call runs.

Honest limitations

  • The Firebase checks are best-effort and may lag behind rule changes.
  • No search or export yet.
  • It is not a no-op in release builds. The panel shows event names and params on screen, which may include user data, so gate it with BuildConfig.DEBUG.
  • The background overlay only lasts while Android keeps your process alive.

Feedback I'd love

  1. Would you use this, and what would stop you?
  2. Is the wrapper approach the right way to avoid double calls, or would you prefer something else?
  3. Search/filter and "share log as text" are next. Is anything more important?

Links

  • GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/JpOriginDev/event-box
  • Issues and PRs welcome.
